verdict.root_cause: At 17:46:31 platform-automation lowered the memory limit on frauddetection-service to 200m and, unlike the four prior lower/restore cycles in the preceding ~16 hours, never restored it [tr_00af10dbdab5]. Thirteen seconds later the JVM entered a restart loop — rapid cycles at 17:46:44/49/58 settling into a near-exact ~62s cadence through 17:53:46, with no exception, stack trace or shutdown message, and no record-consumption lines after the loop began, though the service had been consuming orders normally through 17:23:29 [tr_f1338640f50d]. A JVM that reaches its agent banner and then dies silently on a fixed external cadence immediately after its memory ceiling is cut to 200m is being killed for exceeding that ceiling. The 17:52:15 alert falls mid-loop, not at onset [tr_f1338640f50d].
verdict.reasoning: Two channels converge on the same minute: the only unpaired change in the window is the 200m memory lowering at 17:46:31 [tr_00af10dbdab5], and the crash loop begins 13 seconds later [tr_f1338640f50d]. The silence is diagnostic — startup banners followed by nothing, no application error and no orderly shutdown, is what an external kill looks like from inside the container, and the ~62s regularity implies a supervisor rather than an irregular application fault [tr_f1338640f50d]. Deploys, flags and human edits are absent from the change history [tr_00af10dbdab5]; agent-load failure is excluded because the agent logs its version every cycle [tr_f1338640f50d]. I class this resource_exhaustion rather than bad_config because the edit is how it started while being killed for needing more memory than allowed is what is happening now. Confidence is medium: the metric channel returned nothing usable and the container series that would settle the mechanism were never queried [tr_49b52a82cc0e].
open_questions: No container/kubelet evidence was collected — last-terminated-reason, memory working set against the 200m ceiling, and restart counter are all unretrieved [tr_49b52a82cc0e]; OOMKill is inferred from timing and log shape, not observed.
Why the automation applied the limit a fifth time and omitted its usual restore is unknown, which determines whether this self-heals.
Blast radius beyond frauddetectionservice was not measured; the service has consumed no order records since 17:46 [tr_f1338640f50d].

alternatives.root_cause: A liveness probe is killing each container because a startup dependency became slow, so instances never reach ready before the probe deadline.
alternatives.why_not: Explains the silent ~62s kill cadence equally well, but nothing explains why it would begin 13 seconds after an unpaired memory-limit reduction [tr_00af10dbdab5]; no dependency was investigated, so this survives only as unexamined.

alternatives.root_cause: 200m is below this JVM's irreducible footprint, so the container can never start regardless of load — the wrong value is itself the mechanism.
alternatives.why_not: The process reaches its agent banner every cycle [tr_f1338640f50d], reading as running-then-killed rather than unable-to-initialize; the remediation is identical either way.

proposal.expected_effect: Restoring the configuration in force before 2026-09-06T17:46:31 (memory limit unset, as it was after each of the four prior restores) and recreating the container should end the restart loop. Observable in Loki on {service="frauddetection-service"}: the three-line JVM startup sequence (JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS / CDS warning / OpenTelemetry javaagent version) should appear exactly once after the recreate and then stop recurring on the ~62s cadence seen at 17:47:41-17:53:46; and 'Consumed record with orderId: ... updated total count to: N' lines should reappear with a monotonically advancing counter resuming from the last value near 597, within about 90s of the recreate. Container restart counter, if queried, should stop incrementing.
proposal.if_wrong: Falsified if, more than two cadence periods (~150s) after the recreate, the startup triple is still repeating at ~62s intervals and no record-consumption lines have appeared — that would mean the kill is not driven by the 200m ceiling (the mechanism was inferred from timing and log shape only; last-terminated-reason, working-set vs. limit, and restart count were never retrieved [tr_49b52a82cc0e]). Also falsified in a different way if the loop stops but change-log shows platform-automation re-applying the 200m limit within minutes and the loop returns: then the revert is correct but not durable, and the automation itself — outside what this system may touch — is the thing to fix. Note the span-derived error-ratio series is empty for this service in both incident and baseline windows, so recovery cannot be confirmed from that metric; confirmation must come from logs and container restart counters.
proposal.risk: If the 200m ceiling was applied deliberately to contain a genuine memory leak or runaway allocation in frauddetectionservice, removing it lets the JVM grow unbounded again and shifts the failure from a contained crash-loop to host-level memory pressure, which is worse and hits neighbours rather than one service. If the automation's fifth lowering was a correct response to something we cannot see, this reverts that response. The recreate is also disruptive on its own: in-process state and cache are discarded and the Kafka consumer reconnects, so a brief re-read or gap at the consumer offset is possible. If the diagnosis is wrong the loop simply continues and we have spent one recreate and some minutes.
proposal.blast_radius: One service, frauddetectionservice, plus its callers during the container recreate — though it has been consuming no order records since 17:46, so callers are already seeing total failure and the recreate adds little. On success, the resumed consumption drains an accumulated order backlog, which is a load step for whatever frauddetectionservice reads from and writes to. The brief names no inbound edges and states blast radius beyond frauddetectionservice was not measured [tr_f1338640f50d], so downstream effect is asserted, not observed; approver should confirm the dependency graph before acting.
